hints: For the particle to remain at rest with the least value of $T$, it is on the point of slipping down the plane, so limiting friction $F$ acts up the plane.
Resolve perpendicular to the inclined plane: $R + T\sin 15^\circ = 0.2g\cos 30^\circ \implies R = 2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ$.
Express limiting friction as $F = \mu R = 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ)$.
Resolve parallel to the plane: $T\cos 15^\circ + F = 0.2g\sin 30^\circ$, substitute for $F$, and solve for $T$.
walkthrough: For the least value of $T$, the particle is on the point of slipping downwards, so limiting friction $F$ acts upwards parallel to the plane.

Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane:
$$R + T\sin 15^\circ = mg\cos 30^\circ \implies R = 0.2(10)\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ = 2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ$$
$$R = \sqrt{3} - T\sin 15^\circ \approx 1.73205 - T\sin 15^\circ$$

Express limiting friction in terms of $T$:
$$F = \mu R = 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ) = 0.6\cos 30^\circ - 0.3T\sin 15^\circ$$

Resolve forces parallel to the inclined plane in limiting equilibrium:
$$T\cos 15^\circ + F = mg\sin 30^\circ$$
$$T\cos 15^\circ + 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ) = 0.2(10)\sin 30^\circ$$
$$T(\cos 15^\circ - 0.3\sin 15^\circ) + 0.6\cos 30^\circ = 2\sin 30^\circ$$
teacher_walkthrough: Identify the physical situation: we seek the minimum pulling force $T$ to prevent the particle from sliding down. Therefore, motion is impending down the plane, meaning limiting friction $F = \mu R$ acts upwards along the incline.

Resolve perpendicular to the plane surface:
$$R + T\sin 15^\circ - mg\cos 30^\circ = 0$$
$$R = 0.2 \times 10 \times \cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ = 2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ$$

Apply the limiting friction law with $\mu = 0.3$:
$$F = \mu R = 0.3\left(2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ\right)$$

Set up the equilibrium condition along the line of greatest slope:
$$\Sigma F_{\parallel} = 0 \implies T\cos 15^\circ + F - mg\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$T\cos 15^\circ + 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ - T\sin 15^\circ) = 2\sin 30^\circ$$

Expand and group the terms containing $T$ on the left-hand side:
$$T\left(\cos 15^\circ - 0.3\sin 15^\circ\right) = 2\sin 30^\circ - 0.6\cos 30^\circ$$

Divide by the coefficient of $T$:
$$T = \frac{0.480385}{0.888280} \approx 0.540792\text{ N} = 0.541\text{ N} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

hints: Calculate potential energy lost sliding $3\text{ m}$ down the $30^\circ$ plane: $\Delta E_p = mgh = 0.2(10)(3\sin 30^\circ) = 3\text{ J}$.

Calculate normal reaction $R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 2\cos 30^\circ$, friction force $F = 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ) = 0.6\cos 30^\circ$, and work done against friction: $W_f = 0.6\cos 30^\circ \times 3 \approx 1.5588\text{ J}$.
Calculate work done against the $0.25\text{ N}$ opposing force: $W_T = 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75\text{ J}$.
Apply the work-energy balance: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \Delta E_p - W_f - W_T = 3 - 1.5588 - 0.75 = 0.6912\text{ J}$, and solve for $v$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost as the particle descends $3\text{ m}$ down the $30^\circ$ slope:
$$\Delta E_p = mg(3\sin 30^\circ) = 0.2(10)(3 \times 0.5) = 2(1.5) = 3\text{ J}$$

Calculate the normal reaction and the work done against friction over the $3\text{ m}$ distance:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 0.2(10)\cos 30^\circ = 2\cos 30^\circ$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.3(2\cos 30^\circ) = 0.6\cos 30^\circ$$
$$W_{\text{friction}} = F \times d = (0.6\cos 30^\circ) \times 3 = 1.8\cos 30^\circ \approx 1.8(0.866025) \approx 1.55885\text{ J}$$

Calculate the work done against the opposing $0.25\text{ N}$ force:
$$W_{\text{force}} = 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy principle to determine the final kinetic energy:
$$E_k = \Delta E_p - W_{\text{friction}} - W_{\text{force}}$$
$$\frac{1}{2}(0.2)v^2 = 3 - 1.55885 - 0.75 = 0.69115\text{ J}$$

Solve for the final speed $v$:
$$0.1v^2 = 0.69115 \implies v^2 = 6.9115$$
$$v = \sqrt{6.9115} \approx 2.62898\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 2.63\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the work-energy principle for motion down the rough incline:
$$\text{Final KE} = \text{Loss in PE} - \text{Work Done Against Friction} - \text{Work Done Against Opposing Force}$$

Compute the loss in gravitational potential energy:
$$h = 3\sin 30^\circ = 3 \times 0.5 = 1.5\text{ m}$$
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = 0.2 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 3\text{ J}$$

Compute the work done against friction:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 0.2 \times 10 \times \cos 30^\circ = 2\cos 30^\circ\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.3 \times 2\cos 30^\circ = 0.6\cos 30^\circ\text{ N}$$
$$W_{\text{friction}} = F \times d = 0.6\cos 30^\circ \times 3 = 1.8\cos 30^\circ \approx 1.55885\text{ J}$$

Compute the work done against the constant $0.25\text{ N}$ force:
$$W_{\text{force}} = F_{\text{applied}} \times d = 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75\text{ J}$$

Divide both sides by $0.1$ and solve for $v$:
$$v^2 = \frac{0.69115}{0.1} = 6.9115$$
$$v = \sqrt{6.9115} \approx 2.62898\text{ m s}^{-1} = 2.63\text{ m s}^{-1} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$
